confection

/kun-FEK-shun/ - rhymes with section · noun

Hear It

What It Means

Confection means a sweet, elaborately made food.

The wedding's confection took two days to build and four minutes to disappear.

Example

Every December the corner bakery gives its window to one confection: a sleigh of gingerbread and dark chocolate, harnessed to marzipan reindeer with candied-cherry noses, gliding on drifts of royal icing. Children fog the glass over it all month, and on the twenty-fourth the baker raffles it off for the food pantry.

Confection is the exact word for that sleigh, because a confection is a sweet, elaborately made food — and the stress falls on made. A treat is anything sweet in the hand; a confection is sugar with a blueprint behind it, food somebody engineered.

Compare the words

Synonyms · words with a similar meaning

treat: A treat is anything sweet you are glad to get — a candy bar counts, so does one free cookie — and the word says nothing about workmanship. A confection is built: sugar with a blueprint behind it, assembled to be admired before it is eaten. Every confection is a treat; few treats earn the name confection.

dainty: A dainty is an old-fashioned word for a choice small sweet — the sort passed around on a tea tray, prized for being delicate and little. A confection can be enormous; what earns that name is not the size of the sweet but the craft and elaborate making behind it.

What it isn’t · antonyms and near-opposites

staple: plain food you live on

gruel: food at its most joyless

Where it sits · how much artistry goes into the sweet — snack → dessert → confection

snack vs. confection: A snack is far plainer than a confection — grabbed, not made, sweetness with no ambition at all, while a confection is sugar somebody engineered to be admired.

dessert vs. confection: Dessert goes further than a snack — a course in its own right — but it stops short of confection, which is sugar with architecture: built to be admired before it is eaten.

Build the Word

The pieces

Prefix — con-

Prefix — con-: together

Root — fect

Root — fect: made (Latin facere)

Suffix — -ion

Suffix — -ion: the act or result of

Put it together

Put it together: Con- (together) + fect- (made) + -ion (the result of) = a thing made up together, assembled from parts with care. Latin conficere covered any careful preparation; English narrowed the word to the sweetest kind.

Use the root in a new word: factory

Use the root in a new word: factory: A factory is a making-place — fact- and fect- are the same Latin 'make' wearing two vowels.

Word Building

Word Choice

light / admiring

Confection is for sweets with craft in them — and, stretched, for anything charmingly over-assembled: a confection of a hat. A treat is anything nice in the hand; a dessert is a course at the meal's end. Say confection when the making is the point.
